# Ubbiritherīgāthā (Thig 3.5)
**ID:** Thig 3.5
**Section:** Therīgāthā (thig)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Ubbiritherīgāthā
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/thig3.5

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ubbiritherīgāthā* (Thig 3.5, verses 51–53) is a short poem belonging to the *Therīgāthā* collection of the Pali Canon [Devdas 2004; SuttaCentral]. The verses center on Ubbirī, described in traditional and narrative contexts as a queen or consort of King Pasenadi of Kosala, who was plunged into overwhelming grief following the death of her young daughter Jīvā [Wijayaratna 1990; Van Gorkom 2009; Horner 1930]. Weeping continuously at the cremation ground in the forest, she is approached by the Buddha, who admonishes her by pointing out that in the vast course of *saṃsāra*, some eighty-four thousand daughters named Jīvā have been burned in that very ground, asking which of them she mourns [Van Gorkom 2009; Perez-Remon 1980; Tsomo 1999]. Hearing this teaching on the universality of death and rebirth, Ubbirī reflects on the Dhamma, lets go of her maternal grief and craving (*taṇhā*), and rejoices that the Buddha has pulled out the painful arrow (*salla*) that pierced her heart [Van Gorkom 2009; Ohnuma 2012]. Modern scholars frequently discuss her poem alongside those of Kisā Gotamī and Paṭācārā as a prominent early Buddhist archetype wherein maternal mourning is universalized to prompt spiritual realization and monastic renunciation [Wijayaratna 1990; Olson 2005; Ohnuma 2012].
No direct cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan are identified by SuttaCentral or DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects significant Pali-internal reuse across three texts: the verses are embedded and commented upon in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* (§2.1–4.1) and the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* (§2.1–2.4) [DharmaNexus]. In addition, DharmaNexus identifies a shared segment between this poem (§1.6–3.4) and the *Pañcasatamattātherīgāthā* (Thig 6.1, §5.1–6.4), where the identical verses describing the extraction of the arrow of grief are shared by the five hundred mourning mothers comforted by Paṭācārā [Ohnuma 2012; DharmaNexus].
**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0509a) (§2.1–4.1 ↔ §775–779); Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0507a) (§2.1–2.4 ↔ §953–954); Pañcasatamattātherīgāthā (Thig 6.1) (§1.6–3.4 ↔ §5.1–6.4)

- [Horner 1930] I. B. Horner, Women under Primitive Buddhism (1930) — Described Ubbirī as a wife of Pasenadi and noted her consolation by the Buddha upon her child's death.

- [Olson 2005] Carl Olson, Different Paths of Buddhism: A Narrative-Historical Introduction (2005) — Mentioned Ubbirī's conversion resulting from grief over the loss of a child.
- [Perez-Remon 1980] Joaquin Perez-Remon, Self and Non-Self in Early Buddhism (1980) — Quoted the Buddha's admonition to Ubbirī bewailing her daughter Jīvā in the forest.
- [Tsomo 1999] Karma Lekshe Tsomo, Buddhist Women Across Cultures (1999) — Reported the Buddha's reminder concerning eighty-four thousand daughters buried in the cemetery.
- [Van Gorkom 2009] Nina Van Gorkom, Abhidhamma in Daily Life (2009) — Detailed the narrative of Ubbirī mourning her daughter Jīvā and the Buddha's verse in the cemetery.
- [Wijayaratna 1990] Mohan Wijayaratna, Buddhist Monastic Life According to the Texts of the Theravada Tradition (1990) — Identified Ubbirī as a wife of King Pasenadi mourning her daughter Jīvā before entering the monastic community.
